analysis.one_liner: Would have rewritten workplace safety law to cut inspections, slash fines, and abolish health research.
analysis.headline: The OSHA rollback bill drew 155 cosponsors — 150 of them Republicans — but never reached a House vote, dying in subcommittee when the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have rewritten the nation's main workplace safety law. It would have made new safety standards much harder to issue by requiring industry-by-industry cost-benefit and risk studies, exempted many small employers from routine inspections, cut maximum fines, and let employers cite "employee misconduct" as a defense. It would also have abolished the government's occupational health research agency (NIOSH) and the Mine Safety and Health Administration, and let many employers self-certify their workplaces as safe instead of being inspected.
analysis.who_benefits: Employers, especially smaller businesses and mine operators. They would face fewer routine inspections, at least 30 days to fix violations, no penalties for "willful and repeated" violations, fines capped at what the Labor Secretary proposes and reducible by correction costs, and new legal defenses — plus the right to petition to overturn existing safety standards and a 90-day deadline after which a variance request is automatically approved. Mining companies would gain the most: the Mine Safety and Health Administration would be abolished, underground mine inspections would drop to one per year, and sand, gravel, and stone mines would be exempt from key training rules. A new industry of certified private workplace auditors would also be created, with its reviews substituting for government inspections.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Employers, small businesses, and mine operators

how_it_helps.text: Exempts small farms (10 or fewer employees with no labor camp) and any business with 50 or fewer employees whose industry injury rate is below the national average from routine OSHA inspections and enforcement, while keeping only complaint-driven and fatality investigations.
Eliminates penalties for willful and repeated safety violations, caps penalties at what the Secretary proposes, and lets fines be reduced by the employer's cost of fixing the violation.

Requires industry-specific regulatory impact, risk, and cost-benefit analyses before any new or revised standard, and lets any affected employer petition to modify or revoke an existing standard, with court review if the Secretary refuses.

Guarantees employers at least 30 days to correct violations before a citation, adds defenses based on employee misconduct, alternative safety methods, and conflicting federal requirements, and automatically approves a variance if the Secretary does not act within 90 days.
Abolishes NIOSH, the federal agency that researches workplace hazards and occupational disease, along with its research, training, and education programs.

Repeals the core titles of the Federal Mine Safety and Health Act, folds mine safety into OSHA, cuts underground mine inspections to at least one per year, and bars enforcement of existing miner training rules at sand, gravel, surface stone, and similar mines.

Reserves at least half of OSHA's annual budget for voluntary consultation and incentive programs and exempts workplaces that employers self-certify as reviewed — by a private certified auditor or a consultation program — from inspection.
Authorizes employer alcohol and drug testing programs, including pre-employment and random testing, and creates a protected channel for employer-run employee safety committees under labor law.

analysis.who_pays: Workers. Employees at exempted small businesses and farms would lose routine safety inspections; miners would lose the dedicated Mine Safety and Health Administration and most of their inspection frequency; the country would lose NIOSH research into occupational disease. Fines for serious hazards would shrink and become harder to impose, and new recordkeeping rules would bar the government from releasing injury data identifying individual employers, reducing the public's ability to see where workers get hurt. Taxpayers would fund a system where at least half of OSHA's budget goes to voluntary programs instead of enforcement.
analysis.who_pays_short: Workers in hazardous jobs and mine communities

drawbacks.text: Weaker enforcement falls hardest on workers with the least power to protect themselves. Exempting small employers with below-average industry injury rates from routine inspection removes oversight precisely where individual workers have the least leverage to demand fixes, and the industry-average exemption could hide dangerous outlier employers within safe industries.

Cutting underground mine inspections to one per year and dissolving MSHA's dedicated enforcement would loosen oversight of one of the country's most dangerous jobs; the Mine Act's separate standards and review structure existed because mining hazards differ from general industry hazards.

Abolishing NIOSH would end federal research that identifies which workplace exposures cause cancer, lung disease, and other illnesses — research that underpins the very standards the bill would make harder to issue.

The bill's core mechanism — replacing inspections with employer self-certification and private audits — has an inherent conflict: the party being regulated would be certifying its own compliance, with no routine government check unless a worker complained or someone died.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill had some good-faith aims: OSHA rulemaking was genuinely slow, some standards imposed costs on small firms out of proportion to their benefits, and voluntary consultation programs can improve safety in cooperative workplaces. But the design went far beyond streamlining. It shifted the system from government enforcement to employer self-certification, stripped the tools (high penalties, willful-violation authority, frequent inspections) that make rules real, and dismantled the research base for future standards. The costs to workers — especially miners and employees of exempted small employers — clearly outweighed the efficiency gains.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to a House committee, got three subcommittee hearings in the summer of 1995, was never voted on by the full committee or the House, and expired when the Congress ended in January 1997.

narrative.text: Rep. Cass Ballenger introduced the bill on June 14, 1995, with more than 60 original cosponsors, including senior House Republicans such as Newt Gingrich's lieutenants Tom DeLay and Dick Armey-era leaders Boehner and Hastert.
The bill was referred to the House Committee on Economic and Educational Opportunities and then to its Subcommittee on Workforce Protections.
The subcommittee held three hearings on the bill, on June 20, June 28, and July 27, 1995, but the full committee never marked it up or voted to send it to the floor.
It gathered 155 cosponsors — 150 Republicans and 5 Democrats — but no floor vote ever came, and the bill died when the 104th Congress ended on January 3, 1997.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Workers kept the existing OSHA and mine safety structure — the inspections, penalty authority, and NIOSH research the bill would have removed all stayed in place. The employers who backed the rollbacks gained nothing.

sides.party_line_note: Of 155 cosponsors, 150 were Republicans and only 5 were Democrats, and all hearings happened in a Republican-controlled committee; no floor vote ever occurred.

industries.note: The bill would have cut inspection frequency, capped and reduced fines, added defenses against citations, and created a path to overturn existing standards — all at the direct expense of the workers those rules protect.

It would abolish MSHA and the Mine Act's enforcement structure, cut underground inspections to once a year, and exempt sand, gravel, and stone mines from training requirements — loosening oversight of the country's most dangerous workplaces.

industries.industry: Private workplace safety auditors and certifiers
industries.note: The bill creates a government-certified private auditing industry whose reviews would substitute for OSHA inspections, giving auditors a permanent, publicly funded role as the gatekeepers of workplace safety.
Authorizing employer testing programs, including pre-employment and random testing, would expand demand for testing services, though the bill frames testing as safety-related rather than punitive.
Abolishing NIOSH would end the federal research program that identifies workplace hazards and underpins future safety standards.
